common_name: Lace Time Cranesbill (White-to-Pink Veined Oxonianum Geranium)

planting.note: Set divisions or container-grown plants in spring into moderately fertile soil that drains well in winter; clumps fill in quickly and can be lifted and divided once congested.

directions: Lace Time opens white in spring, with each petal etched in fine purple veins that deepen to pink as the flower ages, giving a single clump a two-tone, lacy look over many weeks. Plant in sun to partial shade in any reasonably fertile soil that does not sit wet over winter, and expect bloom from mid-spring clear into autumn. Shear the whole plant back by half after the first flush to remove tatty foliage and spent stems, which prompts a tidy rebloom. Established clumps spread into effective, weed-smothering ground cover and divide easily in spring or fall.

common_name: Southcombe Double Cranesbill (Salmon-Pink Double-Flowered Oxonianum Geranium)
scientific_name: Geranium x oxonianum f. thurstonianum 'Southcombe Double'

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moderately fertile, medium-moisture soil with good drainage; this selection stays compact and rarely needs division for vigor alone.

directions: Southcombe Double carries salmon-pink flowers that open nearly single in late spring, then thicken with extra petaloid stamens through summer for a fuller, powder-puff look on the same plant. It stays compact compared to many oxonianum cranesbills, forming a tidy mound of finely cut, faintly blotched green leaves. Grow in full sun to part shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil, and expect one of the longest bloom seasons among the hardy geraniums, often running from late spring until frost. Cut back hard if growth becomes floppy in midsummer to encourage fresh foliage and a second flush of flowers.

common_name: Victor Reiter Meadow Cranesbill (Purple-Edged Foliage Blue-Flowered Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in sun to light shade; foliage color and compactness are best maintained with reliable moisture and good light.

directions: Victor Reiter is a vegetatively propagated selection out of a seed strain raised by California plantsman Victor Reiter, prized for foliage that emerges deep purple in spring and matures to green edged in purple through summer. Dark royal-blue, cup-shaped flowers open atop the mounded clump in early to midsummer, standing out against the tinted leaves. Grow in sun to light shade in reliably moist, well-drained soil, and cut the whole plant back after the main flush to refresh its color and shape. It goes dormant in winter and resents prolonged summer drought, so even moisture keeps it looking its best.

common_name: Sylvia's Surprise Cranesbill (Fuchsia-Pink White-Striped Wallich Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into fertile, well-drained soil; trailing stems benefit from a little support or room to spill over a border edge.

directions: Sylvia's Surprise is a naturally occurring sport of the light-blue 'Buxton's Variety' discovered in a Wrexham garden in 1999, and it keeps that parent's long bloom season while swapping in notched, fuchsia-pink flowers brushed with white at the center. The trailing, wrinkled-leaved stems scramble outward through summer and into fall without becoming invasive, making it useful at the front of a border or tumbling over a low wall. Grow in sun to partial shade in reliably moist, well-drained soil, and shear lightly in midsummer if stems sprawl too far. Foliage often takes on red tones as autumn nights cool.

common_name: Crystal Lake Cranesbill (Lavender-Mauve Veined Wallich Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in full sun to light shade; this selection tolerates drier soil once established better than most wallichianum cultivars.

directions: Crystal Lake was raised in the Netherlands in 2002 from self-pollinated seed of 'Silvery Blue' and carries large crystalline lavender-mauve flowers, each petal washed white at the base and finely veined in purple. It blooms over an exceptionally long window, typically from midsummer until the first hard frost, on a dense, spreading mound of lobed leaves. Grow in full sun for the best flower count, in well-drained soil; once established it handles short dry spells better than many hardy geraniums. Trim lightly in late summer if the mound becomes loose to encourage fresh growth and continued flowering.

common_name: Phlox of Sheep (Creamy Peach Low-Mounding Annual Phlox)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and press seed onto the surface without covering, since light aids germination; transplant or direct sow after frost danger passes.

directions: Phlox of Sheep forms a low, spreading mound rather than an upright spike, with sweetly scented blooms in soft peach, blush, salmon, and buttercream that ripple across the plant like a flock of wooly sheep. Surface-sow seed since it needs light to germinate, and keep it evenly moist until seedlings establish; once growing, the plant tolerates heat well for an annual phlox. Deadhead lightly to keep the cut-and-come-again blooms going from early summer into fall. Its ground-covering habit and fragrance make it a favorite for edging and cutting gardens alike.

common_name: Cecily Annual Phlox (Dwarf Compact Mixed-Color Phlox)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and press seed onto the surface without covering, since light aids germination; set out or direct sow once frost danger has passed.

directions: Cecily is a dwarf, compact strain of annual phlox bred for tidy mounds covered in flat, five-petaled flowers across a mix of bright shades. Its low stature and even habit make it well suited to the front of a border, rock gardens, and containers where taller garden phlox would flop. Surface-sow since the seed germinates best in light, keep the bed evenly moist, and expect continuous bloom from late spring through summer into fall. Shear plants back by a third in midsummer if they stall in the heat to refresh flowering for autumn.

common_name: Bubble Gum Moss Phlox (Bright Pink Dark-Centered Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Set container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or early fall into sharply drained soil; this patented sport is propagated only vegetatively, not from seed.

directions: Bubble Gum arose as a spontaneous branch sport on 'Candy Stripe' and was patented for its bright pink flowers ringed with a dark wine-purple eye around the throat, borne in dense clusters that smother the needle-like foliage each spring. It forms a tight, mat-forming evergreen carpet that spills attractively over rock walls and raised beds. Grow in full sun in sharply drained, lean soil, since rich or wet conditions encourage rot and floppy growth. Shear lightly right after bloom to keep the mat dense and to encourage occasional rebloom later in summer.
